rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine name became a unique proper form whose article is treated as part of the word, as the vocative يا الله shows; its formation has no parallel among ordinary names.
rows.anchor: هذه الطريقة في العلمية التي عرضت لاسم الجلالة لا نظير لها في الأعلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf's derivation of Allah from al-ilah is well supported: the poet's fixed expression معاذ الإلاه shows speakers treated al-ilah as the name's source, with variation only in the form's letters.
rows.anchor: علمنا أنهم يعتبرون الإلاه أصلا للفظ الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet's use of لاه and fixed expressions such as لله أبوك support treating لاه as a shortened form of Allah.
rows.anchor: لاه أبوك لأن هذا مما لزم حالة واحدة

rows.speaker: الجوهري عن سيبويه
rows.claim: One proposed origin is لاه, a verbal noun meaning that God is hidden, with the definite article added to suggest the original sense.
rows.anchor: أن أصله لاه مصدر لاه يليه ليها إذا احتجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposal derives the name from ولاه, meaning one overcome by bewilderment; its initial wāw became hamza and the hamza was later dropped.
rows.anchor: أن أصله ولاه بالواو فعال بمعنى مفعول من وله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further proposal takes the divine name from Syriac لاها, adapted by dropping its final alif and adding Arabic ال.
rows.anchor: أن أصله ( لاها ) بالسريانية علم له تعالى

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj, with the view also attributed to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, holds that Allah was coined directly as God's name rather than derived from أله.
rows.anchor: وقد قال بهذا جمع منهم الزجاج ونسب إلى الخليل وسيبويه

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf says all Arabs pronounce the divine lām emphatically, and their agreement shows the practice was inherited.
rows.anchor: وعلى ذلك ( أي التفخيم ) العرب كلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse puts الحمد before لله because praise for revelation and Islam frames the opening recitation; contextual importance can precede God's intrinsic priority, while praising Him still attends to His affairs.
rows.anchor: فكان المقام للاهتمام به اعتبارا لأهمية الحمد العارضة

rows.speaker: التلمساني
rows.claim: Al-Tilimsani reports a group of scholars who refrain from explaining the divine name out of reverence and because discussion requires scriptural permission; Ibn Ashur calls this an astonishing opinion.
rows.anchor: القول بأن اسم الجلالة يمسك عن الكلام في معناه نعظيما وإجلالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: رب العالمين apposes God's name: praise first recognizes His intrinsic worth, then this description adds His descriptive worthiness for praise.
rows.anchor: وصف لاسم الجلالة فإنه بعد أن أسند الحمد لاسم ذاته تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four descriptions that follow signal that each attribute also merits praise and distinguish God from the idols, objects, and elements other peoples worship.
rows.anchor: وقد أجرى عليه أربعة أوصاف هي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: رب may be a verbal noun or an adjective from upbringing, meaning one who nurtures and directs; tarbiya gradually brings something to its perfection. It may also derive from ownership, with an intensive or rare adjectival form.
rows.anchor: والرب إما مصدر وإما صفة مشبهة على وزن فعل من ربه يربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur prefers deriving رب from nurturing and directing: it suits God's governance and gradual completion of creatures, and avoids redundancy with ملك يوم الدين; one could answer that the worlds here mean only this world.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أنه مشتق من ربه بمعنى رباه وساسه

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf limits رب here to master or king, allowing either a verbal noun or adjective, because the word most commonly carries those meanings.
rows.anchor: إلا أن قرينة المقام قد تصرف عن حمل اللفظ على أكثر موارده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Arabs reserved رب for God is false: they used it for human rulers and masters, idols, and particular possessions; الربّة was a name for al-ʿUzza and أرباب is plural.
rows.anchor: أما إطلاقه على كل من آلهتهم فلا مرية فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic expressions about Joseph's master and the rival lords show that رب can refer to someone besides God; the term remained available in Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: إنه ربي أحسن مثواي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hadith discouraging a person from calling a human master ربي is an etiquette rule to prevent suspected association; possessive phrases such as رب الدار remain permissible.
rows.anchor: وهو نهي كراهة للتأديب ولذلك خص النهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عالم names a class of beings, perhaps because each class marks itself out or enables knowledge of its maker; the form suggests an instrument, and its rational plural gives rational beings precedence over other classes.
rows.anchor: لأن كل جنس له تميز عن غيره فهو له علامة

rows.speaker: التفتزاني
rows.claim: Al-Taftazani defines عالم as knowledgeable beings or any species by which the Creator is known, not a singular name for everything besides God; Ibn Ashur endorses this as accurate Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: العالم اسم لذوي العلم ولكل جنس يعلم به الخالق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The article in العالمين is exhaustive because the context supplies neither an external nor mental referent; it therefore covers every relevant species and, by implication, its individuals.
rows.anchor: تمحض التعريف للاستغراق لجميع الأفراد دفعا للتحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural العالمين makes exhaustive scope explicit and removes a possible generic or familiar reading; Ibn Ashur rejects the claim among al-Sakkaki's followers that an exhaustive singular is broader than an exhaustive plural.
rows.anchor: بطل ما شاع عند متابعي السكاكي من قولهم استغراق المفرد أشمل

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad, quoted by Ibn al-Anbari in al-Qurtubi's commentary, says الرحمن is a Hebrew loan whose khāʾ became Arabic حاء, citing Jarir's poem.
rows.anchor: أن الرحمن اسم عبراني نقل إلى العربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur finds no evidence that الرحمن is Hebrew: Arabic and Hebrew are sister languages, Arabic may be older, and the pagans' question in 25:60 need not mean the word was non-Arabic.
rows.anchor: ولم يأت المبرد بحجة على ما زعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human mercy begins as a tender inward response that moves a person to kindness and aid; when attributed to God it denotes the outward acts of mercy, not a created emotional state, in keeping with transcendence.
rows.anchor: فأصل الرحمة من مقولة الانفعال وآثارها من مقولة الفعل

rows.speaker: أبو حامد الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali says a person who wants to meet a need but cannot do so may be called compassionate for the feeling, but is deficient; the complete quality produces its effect.
rows.anchor: الذي يريد قضاء حاجة المحتاج ولا يقضيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Applying الرحمن الرحيم to God is not ambiguous: common usage makes the intended sense clear, while reason excludes creaturely limitations, as with divine knowledge, life, and power.
rows.anchor: ليس من المتشابه لتبادر المعنى المراد منه بكثرة استعماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scripture uses God's mercy for His willing beneficence to creatures in worldly life, as in 7:156; most divine names similarly carry a scriptural sense freed from creaturely limits.
rows.anchor: فهي منقولة في لسان الشرع إلى إرادة الله إيصال الإحسان

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf and many investigators treat الرحمن as an adjective of enduring quality; a transitive verb can shift to an intransitive habitual form before forming this adjective.
rows.anchor: أن الرحمن صفة مشبهة كغضبان

rows.speaker: ابن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Malik objects to treating الرحمن as an adjective of enduring quality because its source رحم is transitive, and compares it with رب and ملك.
rows.anchor: ومن النحاة من منع أن يكون الرحمن صفة مشبهة

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh treats الرحيم as an intensive form that remains transitive; al-Kashshaf and most scholars instead call it an adjective of enduring quality, though both analyses convey intensity. Ibn Ashur sides with Sibawayh.
rows.anchor: والحق ما ذهب إليه سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both adjectives intensify mercy, but usage supports the principle that added form usually adds force: al-Zajjaj glosses غضبان as full of anger, and Arabs lengthened الشقدف to الشقنداف for a heavier camel litter; the rule has exceptions.
rows.anchor: الزيادة في البناء لزيادة المعنى

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most authorities, including Abu Ubayda, Ibn Jinni, al-Zajjaj, and al-Zamakhshari, consider الرحمن more intense because its form is longer; interpreters explain the pairing by making it more specific and الرحيم broad in its objects.
rows.anchor: قال الجمهور إن الرحمن أبلغ من الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الرحمن is restricted to God, while الرحيم describes mercy reaching many recipients and can also describe the Messenger; therefore the second adjective adds meaning instead of repeating the first.
rows.anchor: ومدلول الرحيم كون الرحمة كثيرة التعلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الرحمن precedes الرحيم because a description of God's intrinsic quality should come before a description of how widely its effects reach.
rows.anchor: لأن الصيغة الدالة على الاتصاف الذاتي أولى بالتقديم

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub treats الرحمن and الرحيم as synonyms and their pairing as emphatic repetition; al-Zajjaj leans toward this view, which Ibn Ashur rejects because emphasis is not warranted here.
rows.anchor: أن الرحمن والرحيم يدلان على معنى واحد

rows.speaker: جمهور الأئمة
rows.claim: Most leading scholars say الرحمن was not used of God by Arabs before Islam; Quranic challenges and repeated Meccan references suggest the name was unfamiliar or contested, and some take it as God's proper name.
rows.anchor: أن وصف الرحمن لم يطلق في كلام العرب قبل الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan verse about what holds the birds uses الرحمن, while the Medinan portion of al-Nahl uses الله, subtly reinforcing the divine name in its Meccan setting.
rows.anchor: ما يمسكهن إلا الرحمن في سورة الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet who called Musaylima رحمانا wrote after Islam during the Yamama revolt; رحمان اليمامة was an extremist title, not evidence of pre-Islamic usage.
rows.anchor: فإنما قاله بعد مجيء الإسلام وفي أيام ردة أهل اليمامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence suits the context: after describing God as the world's nurturer and completer, it names the mercy creatures need from Him as their weak Lord's dependents.
rows.anchor: وكان المربوبون ضعفاء كان احتياجهم للرحمة واضحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although nurture brings creatures toward completion, it can involve hardship; الرحمن assures that God's benefits and laws reach people gently, with ease and without undue burden, including public benefits such as zakat.
rows.anchor: تنبيها على أن تلك النعم الجليلة وصلت إلينا بطريق الرفق واليسر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The grammarians dispute whether an indefinite رحمان takes tanwin; Banu Asad decline all faʿlan forms with a feminine faʿlana, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Radi, and Ibn Malik prefer leaving it uninflected.
rows.anchor: واختار الزمخشري والرضى وابن مالك عدم صرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The judgment-day description answers a risk raised by the preceding mercy: people might use God's care and compassion to excuse neglect of commands, so the verse reminds them that each soul is repaid for what it earned.
rows.anchor: لذلك كان من مقتضى المقام تعقيبه بذكر أنه صاحب الحكم في يوم الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ملِك evokes just rule over subjects, while مالك suggests fitting control of recompense; either counters impunity that might be inferred from the image of a merciful nurturer.
rows.anchor: فأما ملك فهو مؤذن بإقامة العدل وعدم الهوادة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder is needed for listeners who misunderstand mercy, prefer immediate comforts, discount shared benefits, or are overpowered by desire; the final judgment blocks rationalizations for avoiding religious duties.
rows.anchor: فكل هؤلاء مظنة للإعراض عن التكاليف الشرعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placing ملك يوم الدين after رب العالمين الرحمن الرحيم signals that God governs both worldly and afterlife affairs, completing the description.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أنه ولي التصرف في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most reciters read ملك without an alif; Asim, al-Kisa'i, Yaqub, and Khalaf read مالك. Both are established mutawatir readings and are also transmitted from the Prophet and Companions.
rows.anchor: وكلتاهما صحيحة ثابتة كما هو شأن القراءات المتواترة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ملك is an adjective used as a noun for a king, while مالك is the active participle of ملك, owner; the root conveys restraint and control, with الملك governing people and الملك denoting possession of things and their benefits.
rows.anchor: فالأول صفة مشبهة صارت اسما لصاحب الملك

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن السراج
rows.claim: Ibn Siraj rejects the report that Marwan was the first to read ملك يوم الدين because transmitted reports contradict it; the original claim may mean first in a particular town.
rows.anchor: فردّه أبو بكر بن السراج بأن الأخبار الواردة تبطل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because both readings are annexed to يوم الدين, they equally mean that God controls that day's affairs without a partner; interpreters overstate their difference by isolating ملك and مالك from this context.
rows.anchor: فأما والكلمة مضافة إلى يوم الدين فقد استويا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: يوم الدين is the Resurrection and beginning of the afterlife; الدين here means recompense, as al-Find al-Zamani's poem uses دانوا for requiting an earlier deed.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو المعنى المتعين هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God Lord of all contrasts the tribal and national gods people claimed, such as those of Moses, Thaqif's al-Lat, and the Ansar's Manat before Islam.
rows.anchor: فقد كانت الأمم تتخذ آلهة خاصة لها

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report in al-Muwatta says the Ansar before Islam used to worship Manat at al-Mushallal; Ibn Ashur cites it as evidence for localized deities.
rows.anchor: كان الأنصار قبل أن يسلموا يهلون لمناة الطاغية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's rule of the day of recompense is absolute over every creature and begins the endless afterlife, exceeding the grandest human royal titles.
rows.anchor: وهو الذي لا ينتهي ملكه ولا ينقضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling it يوم الدين rather than the day of accounting highlights repayment proportionate to good and evil deeds and pure justice, with no injustice, a mark of the finest kingship.
rows.anchor: لأن إيثار لفظ الدين ( أي الجزاء ) للإشعار بأنه معاملة العامل

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nabigha praises a ruler for repaying good with good and denial with denial, presenting balanced, nonoppressive treatment as a royal virtue.
rows.anchor: وكم جزانا بأيد غير ظالمة عرفا بعرف وإنكارا بإنكار

rows.speaker: الحارث بن حلزة
rows.claim: Al-Harith ibn Hilliza praises Amr ibn Hind as a just ruler whose judgment exceeds that of other men.
rows.anchor: ملك مقسط وأفضل من يم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence of divine attributes hints that God deserves complete praise: the qualities attached to the one praised fit the act of praising in this context.
rows.anchor: إيماء بأن موصوفها حقيق بالحمد الكامل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After completing praise, the speaker turns to God in an initial independent address, showing exclusive devotion through worship and seeking help in recognition of God's due.
rows.anchor: انتقالا من الإفصاح عن حق الرب إلى إظهار مراعة ما يقتضيه حقه

rows.speaker: حسان بن ثابت
rows.claim: Al-Isfahani transmits Hassan's story of a poet calling out praise around al-Numan's pavilion; al-Numan recognized al-Nabigha and admitted him, illustrating the Arabic custom of praising a ruler before addressing him.
rows.anchor: روى أبو الفرج الأصفهاني عن حسان بن ثابت

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most rhetoricians define iltifat as shifting the same referent among first, second, and third person; al-Sakkaki instead defines it as choosing a person-form other than the contextually apt one.
rows.anchor: أحدهما رأي من عدا السكاكي من أئمة البلاغة

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: Al-Sakkaki counts apostrophe to one's own heart as iltifat, whereas other rhetoricians classify Alqama's example as tajrid; Ibn Ashur explains the difference in their definitions.
rows.anchor: فهذا ليس بالتفات عند الجمهور وهو معدود من الالتفات عند السكاكي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proper name counts as third-person reference on both definitions, so the turn from God's name and attributes to إياك is iltifat for both schools.
rows.anchor: أن الاسم الظاهر معتبر من قبيل الغائب على كلا الرأيين

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: Iltifat refreshes listeners by varying expression, like varying flavors for guests; rhetoricians also find additional contextual subtleties in individual shifts.
rows.anchor: بتجديد الأسلوب تجديد نشاط السامع كي لا يمل من إعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the worshipper, carried to the limit of reflection by praising God's greatness, imagines himself in the divine presence and turns to address Him directly.
rows.anchor: فتخيل نفسه في حضرة الربوبية فخاطب ربه بالإقبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Bashir's poem illustrates the reverse shift: after addressing himself, the speaker describes his deficient judgment in third person, as if the self had receded from view.
rows.anchor: فالتفت من خطابه إلى التعبير عنه بضمير الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran's shift in 29:23 stigmatizes the disbelievers by naming their rejection of God's signs before reporting their despair of His mercy.
rows.anchor: بأنهم كفروا بآيات صاحب ذلك الاسم الجليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address also moves naturally from praise into supplication, which requires direct address and leads into the request guide us to the path.
rows.anchor: أنه تخلص من الثناء إلى الدعاء ولا شك أن الدعاء يقتضي الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from third person into first person is natural because the first person is the normal form for things attributed to the speaker.
rows.anchor: إذ هو الأصل في التعبير عن الأشياء المضافة إلى ذات المتكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إياك is an accusative independent pronoun; the stronger analysis treats إيا as a support for a separated pronoun, explaining the attached forms and its use in warnings when the verb is omitted.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أن كلمة إيا جعلت ليعتمد عليها الضمير عند انفصاله

rows.speaker: النحاة
rows.claim: Grammarians offer alternatives: إيا alone is the pronoun and its endings reinforce it; إيا is the pronoun and the following letters clarify it; or it is a noun annexed to pronouns.
rows.anchor: ومن النحاة من جعل ( إيا ) ضميرا منفصلا ملازما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary العبادة is submissive or exceptionally reverent action; obedience is a figurative extension. In religious usage it is whatever pleases God through submission, compliance, and avoidance, including all law.
rows.anchor: وأما إطلاقها على الطاعة فهو مجاز

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says worship means honoring God's commands and caring for creation, the shared purpose of revealed laws despite their differing forms and details.
rows.anchor: العبادة تعظيم أمر الله والشفقة على الخلق

rows.speaker: الصوفية
rows.claim: Sufis distinguish worship, doing what pleases God, from servitude, accepting what God does; other definitions describe servitude as keeping promises and limits, contentment, and patience.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : العبودية الوفاء بالعهود

rows.speaker: الفخر
rows.claim: Fakhr al-Razi ranks worship for reward or fear as low, worship for the honor of belonging to God as intermediate, and worship because God alone deserves it as highest, calling the last servitude.
rows.anchor: مراتب العبادة ثلاث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur rejects devaluing reward-and-fear worship as a Sufi excess: Islam repeatedly encourages it and it is the practice of most believers, though rare people may reach higher motives.
rows.anchor: قد غلب عليه فيه اصطلاح غلاة الصوفية

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Asked why he labored in worship after forgiveness, the Prophet answered that he should be a grateful servant; Ibn Ashur cites this as worship motivated by gratitude, not hope or fear.
rows.anchor: أفلا أكون عبدا شكورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship trains individual and social perfection: it recalls God and recompense, disciplines the self, sustains just relations, and keeps thought on the Creator; this explains the purpose of creation stated in 51:56.
rows.anchor: ظهر أن العبادة هي طريق الكمال الذاتي والاجتماعي مبدأ ونهاية

rows.speaker: ابن سينا
rows.claim: Ibn Sina explains that people need one another, so justice must be maintained by revealed law and a rightful lawgiver; knowledge of the one who rewards good and evil needs repeated worship to preserve it.
rows.anchor: ففرضت عليهم العبادة المذكرة للمعبود ، وكررت عليهم ليستحفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship arises from reverence through love or fear; love is higher because it pleases the worshipper and entails fear of displeasing the beloved, as the cited poems and 3:31 express.
rows.anchor: وأهمه ما كان عن محبة لأنه يرضي نفس فاعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Love-based worship underlies revealed religions and even idolaters' devotion to their gods; some instead worship from fear alone, such as Manicheans who worship Ahriman to avert harm.
rows.anchor: ومن الأمم من عبدت عن خوف دون محبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fronted object in إياك نعبد gives true exclusivity: believers reciting this praise worship God alone.
rows.anchor: حصر حقيقي لأن المؤمنين الملقنين لهذا الحمد لا يعبدون إلا الله

rows.speaker: ابن الحاجب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Hajib argues that fronting the object in إياك نعبد marks emphasis only, not exclusivity, and says the cited exclusivity proofs are weak.
rows.anchor: وزعم ابن الحاجب في ( إيضاح المفصل )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur says Ibn al-Hajib's appeal to فاعبد الله is unconvincing because wording must be judged in its particular context, not treated as equivalent in every passage.
rows.anchor: لا يليق بمقامه العلمي إذ لا يظن أن محامل الكلام متماثلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وإياك نستعين coordinates with إياك نعبد; the clauses are not separated as in a sequence of petitions because the worshippers emphasize both acts in the same exclusive commitment.
rows.anchor: للإشارة إلى خطور الفعلين جميعا في إرادة المتكلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking help means asking another to ease a difficult act through tools, physical cooperation, teaching, advice, or money; seeking God's help concerns what a person cannot achieve alone while still exerting their own ability.
rows.anchor: والاستعانة طلب العون . والعون والإعانة تسهيل فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars divide divine aid into essential capacity and means required for an act, and additional facilitation; the latter is sometimes called tawfiq, which with capacity means creating ability and desire to obey.
rows.anchor: فتنقسم قسمين ضرورية أي ما يتوقف الفعل عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general object of seeking aid is omitted to include all important acts, especially receiving religion and disciplining the soul; the needed knowledge, guidance, laws, and sciences also come from God.
rows.anchor: والمقصود هنا الاستعانة على الأفعال المهمة كلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting إياك نستعين gives hyperbolic, claimative exclusivity: people do help one another, but great matters beyond human aid are sought from God alone. This indirectly rebukes polytheists who worship other beings or use them as intermediaries.
rows.anchor: حصر ادعائي للمبالغة لعدم الاعتداد بالاستعانات المتعارفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indirect rebuke fits those who worship celestial bodies, animals, idols, or other gods and seek their aid as intermediaries to God.
rows.anchor: فهؤلاء جمعوا العبادة والاستعانة بهم لأن جعلهم وسيلة إلى الله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: The Prophet taught Ibn Abbas: when asking, ask God; when seeking help, seek God's help. The grandfather commentator says omitting an explicit exclusivity formula implies that requesting help properly admits no partner, and an explicit restriction would be redundant.
rows.anchor: إذا سألت فاسأل الله وإذا استعنت فاستعن بالله
